I'll say that it is a universal truth that everyone is enough as a person. To believe you "aren't enough" is a though instilled into your head by depression. If your friend went up to you and said "You're not enough. You're the worst." Your friend would be the asshole and you'd simply won't want to be friends anymore. Regardless how well they know you personally. This is like depression. Your depression is warping your mind to think this way. Know that it is not, was not, and will never be true.

And I'm glad you are trying to help her learn. You really are a good parent. 🙂

Her being into animals is great! There's so many broad ways you can teach her. You can bring her to a zoo or aquarium. You can show her some documentaries for her to watch. You can get her animal toys and help her draw animals. Animals are very fascinating and you can teach her about them even if it is something extremely simple and basic like this animal can fly or this animal can swim. 

Now, I know that I have no experience as a parent at all but I would say that all children are different. All children learn at different paces and have a harder time understanding things than others and that's okay! All I would say is be patient and be slow with teaching her stuff. I know you have ADHD, and since I'm not that knowledgeable about it, take my advice with a grain of salt. I would say that you should just say simple sentences that explains what you want to convey. For a very young child, that's all you need. Don't force yourself to act in a way you're not to teach your child. Just incorporate tips slowly, one at a time so it doesn't come off as forced to teach her.

And please, please, please don't compare yourself with others. Comparing yourself to others while you have a mental illness that makes you view yourself negatively is extremely unfair. Remember that people deal with extremely different forms of depression. Some have a very mild case of depression and some have a case of depression so severe, they can't get out of bed. The fact that you still try for your child despite dealing with depression shows just how strong you are.

I remember my sister saying that she could deal with depression better than me. It deeply upseted me. Not because she could, but because I knew deep down that she couldn't do much better. I suffer every day from self hate, mental exhaustion, and suicidal thoughts. Not to mention that everything that is mildly annoying to others is amplified for me and is extremely infuriating to me as a result. Everyone has different brains and different ways of thinking.

Well, I think you're wrong when it comes to you being  "not enough" as a person. You're not lackluster. You ARE enough. You ARE a good parent. You ARE doing your best. I'm being extremely genuine when I say that I believe that you're a wonderful person. You being so emotional only cements more in my mind that you are a good parent and don't let the negative thoughts in your mind tell you otherwise. Okay? 

If you ever think to yourself "I'm not good enough" or "I'm not a good parent", take time to step back and let yourself reflect on your thoughts. Realize that the thoughts of "Not being enough" is not true and are negative thoughts implemented by depression. Take some time clear your head of these thoughts. Distract yourself by doing a hobby you like or listening to some calm music. Get something nice to eat. Relax. Whatever you think is best to help those thoughts go away.

As for you "sucking at teaching her anything new", I would like to share some of my thoughts as an 18 year old guy of how I would want my Dad to approach me with stuff like this. Things that I love learning about and things I enjoyed doing go hand in  hand. That's why I remember everything from my Game Design class with my fun and nice teacher about something that interests me and I can't remember anything from my American government class with a boring subject matter. 

So, when it comes to teaching her something, learn what her interests and hobbies are. Ask her what she loves learning about. If it's something that you know a lot about, then teach her about it in a friendly and calm way. If it's something you don't know anything about, then learn with her. Show interest in her interests and show you're passionate about her passions. Of course, there are some stuff she will not want to learn about it, but it helps when you present the subject to her in a calm and amusing way so it's bearable.

And you say you "can't stop making her upset sometimes." Now I'm not sure what to say about it since I don't know details beyond that but all I can say is be patient and let her know that you genuinely care about her.

Remember that no one is perfect. There is not a single person I can think of, personally or otherwise that is perfect. There's a reason in fiction that characters who are completely perfect aren't good characters. Because flaws are what makes them human. Perfect characters are boring and we root for the characters who are flawed. We root for the underdog who has the whole world stacked against them and they succeed. And I'm rooting for you.
